title: A Rectangle the World Can Share
bigQuestion: How did one short rule book, written in London in 1863, become a game that people in almost every country can play together?

story.title: Two Towns, One Rectangle
story.kicker: Two towns that do not share a language still share a rectangle.
paragraphs: On one side of a border, a team speaks Spanish. On the other side, a team speaks Portuguese. On Saturday they meet on a grass field. The coaches cannot understand each other's words. The players still know exactly where to stand for the start.

Both teams know the white lines. There is a halfway line, a center circle and a goal at each end. The lines come from Law 1 of the Laws of the Game. That law describes the field of play, and it is the same in every country.

The rule book began in London in 1863. It was short enough to print on a few pages. Sailors, students and workers carried copies across oceans. By 1904, soccer groups from seven European countries had formed FIFA in Paris.

Long before that rule book, people in China, Japan and England kicked balls in their own ways. The written laws did not invent kicking. They gave strangers one shared set of rules. That is why two towns without a shared language can play one game.
story.think: What does a written rule book let strangers do that they could not do without it?

lessons.title: Cuju and Kemari
lessons.mainIdea: People in China and Japan played kicking games with a ball many centuries before soccer's rules were written in England.
reading: In ancient China, people played *cuju*. The name means "kick ball." Records show it was played during the Han dynasty, more than 2,000 years ago. Soldiers played it for training, and later it was played at the royal court.
FIFA, the world soccer body, has called cuju the earliest form of football with written evidence. Cuju had its own goals and its own customs. It was not the same game as modern soccer.

In Japan, nobles played *kemari* more than 1,000 years ago. Players stood in a circle and kept a deerskin ball in the air. Kemari is still shown at some Kyoto shrines today. There is no winner in kemari.

words.d: "kick ball"; an old Chinese ball game played more than 2,000 years ago
an old Japanese court game where players keep a deerskin ball in the air

lessons.title: School Rules in England
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, English schools and clubs each wrote their own football rules, which made games between them hard.
reading: In the early 1800s, English boarding schools such as Eton, Harrow and Rugby each played football their own way. Some let players carry the ball. Others did not. Students who went on to university could not agree on one game.

In 1848, students at Cambridge University wrote the *Cambridge Rules*. They wanted players from different schools to share one set of rules. No full copy of the 1848 rules survives, but later versions do.
In 1857, Sheffield Football Club was started in the north of England. It is often called the oldest football *club* still playing. A year later, it wrote the Sheffield Rules for its own games.

words.d: football rules written by students at Cambridge University in 1848
a group of people who join together to play a sport

lessons.title: A London Tavern, 1863
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association was founded at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on October 26, 1863, and it wrote the first laws of association football.
reading: On October 26, 1863, men from about a dozen London clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern. A lawyer named *Ebenezer Cobb Morley* had called the meeting. They founded the *Football Association*, called the FA.
Over several meetings they argued about carrying the ball and kicking other players' shins. In December 1863 they agreed on 13 laws. Those laws said players could not carry the ball in their hands.

The Blackheath club wanted carrying and shin kicking kept, so it left. Clubs that liked carrying later formed the Rugby Football Union in 1871. The FA's game was called *association football*. The word soccer comes from "association."

words.d: England's football body, founded in London on October 26, 1863

the game played under the FA's laws; the full name of soccer

look.title: The first laws

check.why: The first FA laws numbered 13.

check.q: Which word was shortened to make the word soccer?
check.why: Soccer is a short form of association, from association football.

lessons.title: A Board to Guard the Laws
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886 the International Football Association Board, called IFAB, has decided the Laws of the Game.
reading: By the 1880s, England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland each had its own football association. Their rules did not always match. That caused arguments when their teams played each other.
On June 2, 1886, the four associations met in London. They formed the *International Football Association Board*, or *IFAB*. Its job is to keep one set of *Laws of the Game* for everyone.
FIFA joined IFAB in 1913. Today IFAB has eight votes. FIFA holds four, and the four British associations hold one each. A law can change only when at least six of the eight votes agree.

the official rule book of soccer, kept by IFAB

lessons.title: Balls in a Suitcase
lessons.mainIdea: Teachers, students and workers carried the rules of association football to South America in the late 1800s.
reading: British workers, sailors and teachers lived in many port cities in the 1800s. They brought balls and rule books with them. Local people watched, joined in and started their own clubs.

*Alexander Watson Hutton* was a Scottish teacher who moved to Buenos Aires, Argentina. In 1893 he helped found the Argentine Association Football League. He is often called the father of Argentine football.

*Charles Miller* was born in São Paulo, Brazil, in 1874. He went to school in England and learned the game there. In 1894 he came home with footballs and a copy of the rules. He helped start organized soccer in São Paulo.

words.d: a Scottish teacher who helped start organized soccer in Argentina in 1893
a Brazilian who brought footballs and a rule book home to São Paulo in 1894

lessons.title: Seven Nations in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris on May 21, 1904, by football associations from seven European countries.
reading: On May 21, 1904, football leaders met in Paris, France. They founded *FIFA*, the Fédération Internationale de Football Association. In English, that means International Federation of Association Football.

The seven founding members came from France, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland. England's FA joined in 1905. A *federation* is a group of separate bodies that agree to work together.
FIFA agreed to play by the Laws of the Game kept by IFAB. Today FIFA has more than 200 member associations. That is more members than the United Nations has countries.

words.d: the world soccer body, founded in Paris on May 21, 1904
a group of separate bodies that agree to work together

lessons.title: Uruguay Hosts the World, 1930
lessons.mainIdea: The first FIFA World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won the final against Argentina.
reading: FIFA president *Jules Rimet* of France wanted a tournament for national teams. In 1930 the first *World Cup* was held in Uruguay, in South America. That year was the 100th anniversary of Uruguay's first constitution.

Uruguay built the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo for the event. The name means Centenary Stadium. Thirteen teams took part. Only four came from Europe, because the trip by ship took about two weeks.
On July 30, 1930, Uruguay beat Argentina 4 to 2 in the final. The United States team also played and reached the semifinals. Today the World Cup is held every four years.

words.d: FIFA's tournament for national teams, first held in Uruguay in 1930
the French FIFA president who pushed for the first World Cup

lessons.title: Women Shut Out, Then Back
lessons.mainIdea: England's FA banned women's games from its members' grounds in 1921 and did not lift the ban until 1971.
reading: During World War I, many women worked in factories in England. Some formed football teams. The *Dick, Kerr Ladies* came from a factory in Preston. On Boxing Day 1920, about 53,000 people watched them play at Goodison Park in Liverpool.

On December 5, 1921, the FA made a new rule. It said football was "quite unsuitable for females." Member clubs could no longer let women's teams use their grounds. This was a *ban*, a rule that stops people from doing something.
Women kept playing on smaller fields. The FA lifted the ban in 1971. FIFA held the first Women's World Cup in China in 1991. The United States won it.

a rule that stops people from doing something

lessons.title: Law 1: The Field of Play
lessons.mainIdea: Law 1 of the Laws of the Game lets a soccer field be many sizes, as long as it is a rectangle with the right markings.
reading: A soccer field is called a *pitch*. Law 1 of the Laws of the Game describes it. It must be a rectangle. The long sides are touchlines. Each one is a *touchline*. The short sides are goal lines.
Law 1 gives a range of sizes, not one size. A pitch may be 90 to 120 meters long. That lets a village, a school or a big city stadium all follow the same law.

Some parts never change. Every goal is 8 yards wide and 8 feet high, or 7.32 meters by 2.44 meters. Those sizes come from the British measures of the 1800s. They were kept when the laws spread around the world.

one of the two long side lines of a soccer pitch

lessons.title: Chicago and the World Cup
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Soldier Field hosted the opening game of the 1994 World Cup, and U.S. Soccer has its headquarters in Chicago.
reading: In 1994 the United States hosted the men's World Cup for the first time. The opening game was played at *Soldier Field* in Chicago on June 17, 1994. Germany beat Bolivia 1 to 0.
The *United States Soccer Federation*, called U.S. Soccer, runs the sport's national teams. It has had its headquarters in Chicago since 1991. Its offices are in an old mansion on Prairie Avenue.

Chicago also has a professional club, the Chicago Fire. The team is named for the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. It played its first season in 1998 and won Major League Soccer's championship that same year.

words.d: Chicago's lakefront stadium, which hosted the opening game of the 1994 World Cup

lessons.title: State Titles for Boys and Girls
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first boys soccer state champion in 1972 and its first girls soccer state champion in 1988.
reading: Illinois high schools played soccer for years without a state title. The IHSA held its first boys soccer *state series* in the fall of 1972. A state series is a set of playoff rounds that ends with one champion.
Also in 1972, Congress passed *Title IX*. This federal law says schools that get federal money cannot shut students out of programs because of sex. Schools began adding more sports for girls.
Girls soccer grew in Illinois through the 1970s and 1980s. The IHSA crowned its first girls soccer state champion in 1988. Today boys play in the fall and girls play in the spring.
